q: Python searches namespaces in which order?
why: The first namespace holding the name wins, which is why an inner name shadows an outer one for the whole of that scope.

q: Which of these introduces a new scope?
why: Only functions, classes, modules and comprehensions do. A `for` variable outlives its loop and holds the last value.

q: What makes a name local to a function?
options: Assigning to it anywhere in the body
Using it in a nested function
why: And it is local for the whole body, including the lines above the assignment, because the decision is made when the function is compiled.

why: `+=` is an assignment, so `count` is local throughout, so the read finds an unfilled local slot.

q: Inside a method, a bare reference to a class attribute
options: Works, because the class body is an enclosing scope
Raises NameError; the attribute needs `self.` or the class name
Shadows the builtin of that name
why: A class body is a scope but deliberately not an *enclosing* scope for functions defined inside it.

q: Why does a comprehension in a class body fail to see the class's other names?
options: Comprehensions cannot appear in a class body
The comprehension body is an implicit function, and class scope does not enclose functions
The names are not yet defined at that point
It only fails for mutable attributes
why: The first iterable is the exception: it is evaluated in the enclosing scope, which is why `for k in KEYS` works.

q: Why is shadowing a builtin worse than shadowing a local?
options: Builtins are searched last, so the failure appears wherever the builtin is next needed
Builtins cannot be shadowed at all
why: `list`, `dict`, `type`, `id` and `input` are all ordinary names. A trailing underscore is the usual escape.
